title: Jabbo Smith and his lost promise
summary: Cootie admires Jabbo's playing in 1928 and regrets that he dropped out of sight in Milwaukee.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: No. Well, getting away from the job and the location, was there anybody else around town blowing or anything that meant anything to you? Did you go around and blow

No. No -- not very seldom. Because we used to work so hard, and when you got out of work, every place was closed. Or about. The only one I can remember was playing so beautifully, and I'm sorry that he lost all of that.
Who?
And the world lost a great -- Jabbo Smith.
Oh, yeah.
He was blowing beautifully in '28. And he was blowing. He was another trumpet player that was great.
What happened to Jabbo? Was it life got him down or something?
I don't know what happened to him. I know he moved out of New York and went to Milwaukee. And no-one ever heard anything more about him.

You know, in '33, when I was living in Chicago, you know, I was doing some sessions for Brunswick, and I had a -- I got -- I put a band together, and had Jabbo on the session. And he showed up and blew on the first session. And something was wrong with the equipment, or the studio or something, and we had to call the second session, and he never showed up. That was a shame. But he did show up on the first one, and he blew. And I guess he came in from Milwaukee. I
guess that's just what he did.
Yeah, but in '28, that guy was really blowing.
That's a shame, isn't it?
Yeah. It really is a shame. The way that guy was blowing. I don't know what happened to him.
Because he had something different from Louis, didn't he?
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah, he was a great musician. Great jazz player.
And he didn't get to record very much at that, did he?
No.
I don't think he did.
I don't think he did.
